title: Data Handling: Graphs, Pie Charts and Probability
explanation:
Data is information collected about a situation, organised systematically so it can be read and compared, rather than left as a jumble of numbers. A pictograph represents that data using a picture symbol, where each symbol (or a fraction of one) stands for a fixed quantity — for example, one book symbol might mean '2 books read'. A bar graph represents the same kind of data with bars of uniform width, equally spaced, where the height of each bar is proportional to the value it represents — taller means more. A double bar graph places two related bars side by side for each category, which makes it easy to compare two data sets directly, category by category, rather than looking at two separate graphs. One detail that trips students up: if the bars in a bar graph are rearranged — say, from tallest to shortest instead of alphabetical order — the information the graph conveys does not change at all. Only the order in which it's presented changes; every bar still represents the same value it always did.

A pie chart (or circle graph) shows how a whole is split into parts, by dividing a circle into sectors whose sizes are proportional to what they represent — a category that makes up half the data gets a sector that's half the circle. The size of each sector is measured as a central angle, calculated with one formula: central angle = (that part's fraction of the whole) × 360°, since a full circle is 360°. For example, if 'Rent' is 25% of a family's expenses, its sector's central angle is (25/100) × 360° = 90°. To construct a pie chart by hand: draw a circle and mark its centre, draw a starting radius, then use a protractor centred at that point to mark off each sector's angle in turn, moving around the circle. A related, more subtle skill is back-solving: if you're told one sector's real-world value together with its percentage (or angle) of the total, that pair gives you a unit rate — for instance, 'Rent is 25% of the budget and equals ₹5,000' tells you that 1% equals ₹200, so the whole budget (100%) is ₹20,000. That same unit rate can then be used to find the real-world value behind any other sector in the same chart.

A random experiment is one whose result cannot be predicted or controlled in advance, even in principle — tossing a coin or throwing a die are both random experiments, but checking whether the sun will rise tomorrow is not, since that outcome is certain. Each single possible result of an experiment is called an outcome (e.g. getting 'Heads', or rolling a '4'); an event is one outcome or a whole collection of outcomes grouped together (e.g. 'rolling an even number' is the event made up of the outcomes 2, 4, and 6). Outcomes are equally likely when each one has exactly the same chance of happening — this is only true when nothing about the experiment favours one outcome over another (a fair die's six faces are equally likely; a spinner with unequal sector sizes is not). Whenever outcomes are equally likely, probability can be calculated with one formula: P(event) = (number of outcomes that make the event happen) / (total number of equally likely outcomes). Probability isn't just a classroom idea — it's used to make real-world predictions from incomplete information, such as exit polls estimating an election result from a small sample of voters, or weather forecasts estimating tomorrow's conditions from historical patterns. In both cases, the prediction is a likelihood, not a certainty.
workedExampleContent:
A student's weekly pocket money of ₹120 is spent as: Snacks ₹60, Books ₹30, Savings ₹30. Find the central angle of each sector in a pie chart of this data.

Step 1: Find each category's fraction of the total: Snacks = 60/120 = 1/2. Books = 30/120 = 1/4. Savings = 30/120 = 1/4.
Step 2: Multiply each fraction by 360° to get its central angle: Snacks = 1/2 × 360° = 180°. Books = 1/4 × 360° = 90°. Savings = 1/4 × 360° = 90°.
Step 3: Check that the angles add up to 360°: 180° + 90° + 90° = 360°.

Snacks: 180°, Books: 90°, Savings: 90°.

---

A box has 3 red pens, 2 blue pens and 5 black pens, identical except for colour. One pen is drawn without looking. What is the probability of drawing a blue pen?

Step 1: Find the total number of equally likely outcomes: 3 + 2 + 5 = 10 pens.
Step 2: Count the outcomes that make the event 'drawing a blue pen': 2.
Step 3: Apply the probability formula: P(blue) = (favourable outcomes) / (total outcomes) = 2/10.
Step 4: Simplify the fraction: 2/10 = 1/5.

P(blue pen) = 1/5.

title: Solving Linear Equations in One Variable
explanation:
An equation is a statement that says two expressions are equal, written with an '=' sign — for example, 2x + 1 = 7. An expression like 2x + 1 on its own, without an equals sign, is just an expression, not an equation. A linear equation in one variable is an equation where the variable appears only to the power 1 — no x², no x³. The expression on the left of the '=' sign is called the LHS (Left Hand Side), and the expression on the right is the RHS (Right Hand Side). A solution of the equation is the value of the variable that makes the LHS exactly equal to the RHS — not every value works, only specific ones. The reason we can solve equations at all is the balancing principle: if you do the same thing to both sides of an equation — add the same number, subtract the same number, multiply or divide both sides by the same non-zero number — the two sides stay equal. Every method used to solve an equation is really just this one idea, applied step by step.

Sometimes the variable appears on both sides of the equation, like 4x + 5 = 2x + 17. To solve this, we want all the x terms on one side and all the plain numbers on the other. The balancing principle says we can move a term from one side to the other, as long as we flip its sign when it crosses the '=' sign — this shortcut is called transposition. Moving +2x from the right side to the left turns it into -2x there, giving 4x - 2x + 5 = 17, which simplifies to 2x + 5 = 17. From there, transpose the +5 to the right (it becomes -5): 2x = 12, so x = 6. If the equation has a fractional coefficient, like x = (4/5)(x + 10), it helps to first multiply both sides by the denominator to clear the fraction, turning it into a plain integer equation before transposing.

Some equations look more complicated because they contain brackets or several different denominators, like 2(x + 1) = (3x - 1)/2 + 3. Two steps make these manageable. First, if there are denominators, multiply every single term on both sides by their LCM (lowest common multiple) — this clears all the fractions at once, turning the equation into one with only whole numbers. Second, if there are brackets, expand them first: multiply the number outside the bracket by every term inside it, not just the first one. Once fractions are cleared and brackets are expanded, combine like terms and solve using transposition, exactly as before. However an equation was solved, always finish by checking the answer: substitute the value back into the original LHS and the original RHS separately, and confirm the two sides come out equal. This check is what actually proves the answer is correct — it's not an optional extra step.
workedExampleContent:
Is x = 4 a solution of the equation 3x - 5 = 7?

Step 1: Substitute x = 4 into the LHS: 3(4) - 5 = 12 - 5 = 7.
Step 2: The RHS is 7.
Step 3: Compare: LHS = 7 and RHS = 7, so LHS = RHS.

Yes — x = 4 is a solution of 3x - 5 = 7, since both sides equal 7.

---

Solve for x: 4x + 5 = 2x + 17.

Step 1: Transpose 2x from the RHS to the LHS: 4x - 2x + 5 = 17.
Step 2: Simplify the LHS: 2x + 5 = 17.
Step 3: Transpose 5 from the LHS to the RHS: 2x = 17 - 5 = 12.
Step 4: Divide both sides by 2: x = 6.
Step 5: Check: LHS = 4(6) + 5 = 29. RHS = 2(6) + 17 = 29. LHS = RHS, as required.

x = 6.

---

Solve for x: 2(x + 1) = (3x - 1)/2 + 3.

Step 1: Multiply both sides by 2 (the denominator on the RHS) to clear the fraction: 2 × 2(x+1) = 2 × [(3x-1)/2 + 3].
Step 2: Simplify: 4(x + 1) = (3x - 1) + 6.
Step 3: Expand the bracket on the LHS: 4x + 4 = 3x + 5.
Step 4: Transpose 3x to the LHS and 4 to the RHS: 4x - 3x = 5 - 4.
Step 5: Simplify: x = 1.
Step 6: Check: LHS = 2(1 + 1) = 4. RHS = (3(1) - 1)/2 + 3 = 2/2 + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4. LHS = RHS, as required.

x = 1.

title: Rational Numbers: Properties and Operations
explanation:
A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. This is a broad definition — every whole number and every integer is automatically a rational number too, since 5 can be written as 5/1, and −3 as −3/1. The same rational number can be written in more than one way: −4/6, 2/−3 and −2/3 are all the same number, just written with different numerators and denominators. To avoid this ambiguity, a rational number is said to be in standard form when its denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator share no common factor other than 1 — reducing any equivalent fraction down to one canonical version. For example, −4/6 reduces to −2/3 in standard form: divide both numerator and denominator by their common factor of 2, and flip the sign so the denominator stays positive.

Rational numbers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, which means combining any two rational numbers with one of these operations always produces another rational number — you never leave the set. They are not closed under division, because dividing by 0 is undefined. This mirrors what's true of whole numbers and integers, with one difference: integers are also closed under subtraction, while whole numbers are not (5 − 7 = −2 is not a whole number, but it is an integer and a rational number). Addition and multiplication are commutative for rational numbers — the order you combine two numbers in doesn't change the result, so a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a for any rational numbers a and b. Subtraction and division are not commutative: swapping the order generally gives a different answer. The same pattern holds for associativity, which is about grouping rather than order: addition and multiplication are associative, meaning a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c and a × (b × c) = (a × b) × c no matter how the numbers are grouped, but subtraction and division are not associative — regrouping them can change the result.

Zero is the additive identity for rational numbers: adding 0 to any rational number a leaves it unchanged, a + 0 = 0 + a = a. This is the same role zero plays for whole numbers and integers. One is the multiplicative identity for rational numbers in exactly the same way: multiplying any rational number a by 1 leaves it unchanged, a × 1 = 1 × a = a. Distributivity connects addition and multiplication: for any rational numbers a, b and c, a(b + c) = ab + ac, and equally a(b − c) = ab − ac. This isn't just a rule to memorise — it's a genuinely useful calculation shortcut. Instead of adding two fractions first and then multiplying the sum by a third number, you can multiply each piece separately and add the results, whichever order turns out to involve simpler arithmetic. Recognising when an expression fits this pattern is what makes distributivity useful in practice, not just as an abstract property.

Every rational number a has an additive inverse, written −a, which is the number that brings a back to the additive identity: a + (−a) = 0. This is sometimes just called the negative of a number. Flipping the sign of a rational number (positive to negative, or negative to positive) always produces its additive inverse — the additive inverse of 3/8 is −3/8, and the additive inverse of −5/9 is 5/9. Every non-zero rational number a = p/q also has a multiplicative inverse, called its reciprocal, formed by swapping the numerator and denominator: the reciprocal of p/q is q/p, and a × (q/p) = 1 always holds. The reciprocal of a whole number like 5 is 1/5, since 5 = 5/1 and swapping gives 1/5. There's exactly one important exception: 0 has no reciprocal, because no number multiplied by 0 can ever equal 1 — division by zero is precisely the operation that's left undefined.

Rational numbers occupy positions on the number line just like whole numbers and integers do, but far more densely — a rational number with denominator q is found by subdividing the space between consecutive integers into q equal parts. Unlike integers, where the number line has visible gaps (there's nothing between 3 and 4), rational numbers pack every one of those gaps with more rational numbers, and each of those with still more. A simple, reliable way to find a rational number that lies exactly between two given rational numbers a and b is to compute their mean, (a + b) ÷ 2 — this average always lies exactly halfway between them. Repeating this process — taking the mean of the new number and one of the originals — produces yet another rational number in between, and this can be repeated without ever running out. This is why there are infinitely many rational numbers between any two given rational numbers, no matter how close together those two numbers already are — a sharp contrast to integers, where only a finite number (or sometimes none at all) fit between two given values.
workedExampleContent:
Write −18/24 in standard form.

Step 1: Find the greatest common factor of 18 and 24: it is 6.
Step 2: Divide both the numerator and denominator by 6: −18÷6 = −3, 24÷6 = 4.

−18/24 in standard form is −3/4.

---

Show that addition is commutative for −2/5 and 3/7 by computing both sums.

Step 1: Compute −2/5 + 3/7 using a common denominator of 35: (−14 + 15)/35 = 1/35.
Step 2: Compute 3/7 + (−2/5) using the same common denominator: (15 − 14)/35 = 1/35.
Step 3: Both sums equal 1/35, regardless of the order the two numbers were added in.

Both sums equal 1/35, confirming addition is commutative for these two numbers.

---

Use distributivity to compute 5/6 × (2/3 + 1/3).

Step 1: Add the bracketed terms first: 2/3 + 1/3 = 1.
Step 2: Multiply: 5/6 × 1 = 5/6.
Step 3: Check by distributing instead: 5/6×2/3 + 5/6×1/3 = 10/18 + 5/18 = 15/18 = 5/6 — same result either way.

5/6 × (2/3 + 1/3) = 5/6.

---

Find the reciprocal of −4/9, and verify it by multiplying the two numbers together.

Step 1: To find the reciprocal, swap the numerator and denominator, keeping the sign: the reciprocal of −4/9 is −9/4.
Step 2: Verify: −4/9 × −9/4 = 36/36 = 1.

The reciprocal of −4/9 is −9/4.

---

Find a rational number that lies between 1/3 and 2/3.

Step 1: Add the two numbers: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1.
Step 2: Divide the sum by 2 to find their mean: 1 ÷ 2 = 1/2.

1/2 lies exactly between 1/3 and 2/3.

Flipping the sign of a rational number (positive to negative, or negative to positive) always produces its additive inverse — the additive inverse of 3/8 is −3/8, and the additive inverse of −5/9 is 5/9. Every non-zero rational number a = p/q also has a multiplicative inverse, called its reciprocal, formed by swapping the numerator and denominator: the reciprocal of p/q is q/p, and a × (q/p) = 1 always holds. The reciprocal of a whole number like 5 is 1/5, since 5 = 5/1 and swapping gives 1/5. There's exactly one important exception: 0 has no reciprocal, because no number multiplied by 0 can ever equal 1 — division by zero is precisely the operation that's left undefined.

concepts.title: The number line and rational numbers between two rationals
concepts.body: Rational numbers occupy positions on the number line just like whole numbers and integers do, but far more densely — a rational number with denominator q is found by subdividing the space between consecutive integers into q equal parts. Unlike integers, where the number line has visible gaps (there's nothing between 3 and 4), rational numbers pack every one of those gaps with more rational numbers, and each of those with still more. A simple, reliable way to find a rational number that lies exactly between two given rational numbers a and b is to compute their mean, (a + b) ÷ 2 — this average always lies exactly halfway between them. Repeating this process — taking the mean of the new number and one of the originals — produces yet another rational number in between, and this can be repeated without ever running out. This is why there are infinitely many rational numbers between any two given rational numbers, no matter how close together those two numbers already are — a sharp contrast to integers, where only a finite number (or sometimes none at all) fit between two given values.

title: A Square and A Cube: Numbers and Roots
explanation:
A perfect square is any number you get by multiplying a natural number by itself — 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on are all perfect squares, since they equal 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5. One quick way to rule a number out is the unit's-digit test: every perfect square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 can never be a perfect square — but the reverse isn't guaranteed: 26 ends in 6 yet isn't a perfect square, so passing this test only means 'maybe', never 'definitely yes'. A more powerful check is the odd-number-sum test: every perfect square n² is exactly the sum of the first n consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 — 1, 1+3=4, 1+3+5=9, 1+3+5+7=16, and so on. Equivalently, if you successively subtract 1, then 3, then 5, and so on from a number and land exactly on 0, that number is a perfect square; landing on a negative result partway through means it isn't. This same structure tells you how many non-square numbers sit between consecutive squares: between n² and (n+1)² there are always exactly 2n non-square numbers — for example, between 5²(=25) and 6²(=36) there are 2×5=10 non-square numbers. A separate, well-known pattern connects squares to right triangles: for any natural number m greater than 1, the three numbers 2m, m²−1 and m²+1 always form a Pythagorean triplet, meaning the squares of the two smaller numbers add up to the square of the largest. Not every Pythagorean triplet can be built this way, but this formula always produces a valid one.

Finding a square root is the reverse of squaring: if y = x², then x is a square root of y. A perfect square strictly has two integer square roots, one positive and one negative (since (−x)² = x² too), but this course only ever uses the positive one, written with the symbol √. One way to find a square root by hand is repeated subtraction: keep subtracting consecutive odd numbers — 1, then 3, then 5, and so on — from the number, and if you land exactly on 0, the count of subtractions you made is the square root. This works but becomes slow for large numbers, so the more practical method is prime factorisation: break the number down into its prime factors, pair up identical factors, and multiply one factor from each pair together — that product is the square root. If even one prime factor is left without a partner, the number isn't a perfect square at all. This same idea tells you how to *fix* a near-miss: if a number's factorisation has one or more unpaired primes, multiplying by exactly those missing partners (or dividing them out) turns it into a perfect square — this is how you find the smallest number to multiply or divide by. For numbers that aren't perfect squares, you can still estimate the square root by bracketing: find the two consecutive whole numbers whose squares sit just below and just above the target, which pins the square root to that range, and you can narrow the range further by comparing to the midpoint's square. These methods aren't just abstract number theory — finding the side length of a square given its area, or applying the Pythagorean relation to find an unknown side of a right triangle, both come down to computing a square root.

A perfect cube is a number you get by multiplying a natural number by itself three times — 1, 8, 27 and 64 are perfect cubes, since they equal 1×1×1, 2×2×2, 3×3×3 and 4×4×4. Checking whether a number is a perfect cube uses the same prime-factorisation idea as squares, but with triples instead of pairs: break the number into prime factors, and it's a perfect cube only if every single prime factor can be grouped into a complete set of exactly three. If any prime factor's count doesn't divide evenly into groups of three, the number isn't a perfect cube. That incomplete grouping also tells you exactly how to fix it: multiplying by the missing factor(s) completes the triple and produces a perfect cube, while dividing out the excess factor(s) that don't fit a triple does the same. A famous, purely numerical fact about cubes is the Hardy–Ramanujan number, 1729 — it's the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two genuinely different ways: 1³+12³ and 9³+10³ both equal 1729. It's a striking illustration that cube arithmetic can hide unexpected coincidences, discovered by the mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan.

Finding a cube root is the reverse of cubing: if y = x³, then x is the cube root of y, written with the symbol ∛. The most reliable hand method mirrors the square-root technique but works in threes instead of twos: break the number into its prime factors, group identical factors into complete triples, and multiply one factor from each triple together to get the cube root. This method extends naturally to real-world measurement problems — since the volume of a cube is (edge length)³, finding the edge length of a cube from its known volume is exactly the same calculation as finding a cube root by prime factorisation.
workedExampleContent:
Is 128 a perfect square? Use prime factorisation to justify your answer.

Step 1: Prime factorise 128: 128 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁷.
Step 2: Group the factors in pairs: 2⁷ = (2×2) × (2×2) × (2×2) × 2 — one factor of 2 is left unpaired.
Step 3: Since not every prime factor pairs up, 128 is not a perfect square.

No, 128 is not a perfect square — its prime factorisation leaves one 2 unpaired.

---

A square plot of land has an area of 1,764 m². Find the length of one side.

Step 1: The side length is the square root of the area: side = √1764.
Step 2: Prime factorise 1764: 1764 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 7 = 2² × 3² × 7².
Step 3: Pair the factors and multiply one from each pair: √1764 = 2 × 3 × 7 = 42.

The side of the plot is 42 m.

---

Find the smallest number by which 200 must be multiplied to make it a perfect cube.

Step 1: Prime factorise 200: 200 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 = 2³ × 5².
Step 2: Group the factors in triples: 2³ is already a complete triple; 5² needs one more 5 to become 5³.
Step 3: Multiply by the missing factor: 200 × 5 = 1000, which is 10³.

The smallest number is 5; 200 × 5 = 1000 = 10³.

---

Find the cube root of 5832 by prime factorisation.

Step 1: Prime factorise 5832: 5832 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 2³ × 3⁶.
Step 2: Group the factors in triples: 2³ is one triple; 3⁶ splits into two triples (3³ × 3³).
Step 3: Multiply one factor from each triple: cube root = 2 × 3 × 3 = 18.

The cube root of 5832 is 18.

title: Understanding Quadrilaterals: Polygons and Their Properties
explanation:
A polygon is a simple closed figure made up entirely of line segments — 'simple' means its boundary doesn't cross itself, and 'closed' means it has no gaps. A circle or any shape with a curved edge is not a polygon, no matter how it's drawn. Polygons come in two important pairs of categories. First, convex vs. concave: a polygon is convex when every one of its interior angles is less than 180°; if even one angle is greater than 180° — a single 'caved-in' vertex — the whole polygon is concave. Second, regular vs. irregular: a polygon is regular only when it satisfies two conditions at once — all of its sides are equal in length, AND all of its angles are equal in measure. A shape that meets only one of those two conditions (like a rhombus, whose sides are all equal but whose angles usually aren't) is irregular, not regular.

Every polygon's interior angles add up to a fixed total that depends only on its number of sides: for a polygon with n sides, the sum of the interior angles is (n − 2) × 180°. A quadrilateral (n = 4) always has interior angles summing to 360°; a pentagon (n = 5) always sums to 540°; and so on. This formula also works in reverse — if you're told the angle sum, you can solve for n. Alongside this, every convex polygon has a second, even simpler rule: its exterior angles, taken one at each vertex going around in order, always add up to 360° — this is true no matter how many sides the polygon has, unlike the interior sum. At any single vertex, the interior angle and its exterior angle always add up to 180°, since together they form a straight line. For a regular polygon specifically, this gives two useful shortcuts: each exterior angle equals 360° divided by the number of sides, and each interior angle equals (n − 2) × 180° divided by the number of sides.

A trapezium is a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides — those parallel sides are called the bases, and the two non-parallel connecting sides are called the legs. A shape with both pairs of opposite sides parallel isn't a trapezium under this definition; it belongs to the parallelogram family instead, covered next. A kite is a quadrilateral with two distinct pairs of adjacent (side-by-side) sides that are equal in length — unlike a parallelogram, where it's the opposite sides that match, a kite's matching sides are neighbors that share a vertex. A kite's diagonals have their own distinct behavior: they cross at right angles, but only one of the two diagonals is actually cut exactly in half by the other — both diagonals being bisected is a parallelogram property, not a kite property.

A parallelogram is a quadrilateral where both pairs of opposite sides are parallel and equal in length. This one shape gives rise to several more properties worth knowing: opposite angles are equal to each other; two angles that are adjacent (next to each other, sharing a side) are supplementary, meaning they add up to 180°; and the two diagonals bisect each other, crossing at a point that is the exact midpoint of both. Three special parallelograms each add one extra condition on top of all of this. A rhombus is a parallelogram where all four sides are equal — its diagonals bisect each other at right angles, and each diagonal also bisects the pair of angles it passes through. A rectangle is a parallelogram where all four angles are 90° — its diagonals are equal in length, in addition to bisecting each other. A square satisfies both extra conditions simultaneously — all sides equal AND all angles 90° — which makes it both a rhombus and a rectangle at the same time, with diagonals that are equal in length AND bisect each other at right angles. Because of this, there's a one-directional hierarchy worth remembering: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus; every rectangle is a parallelogram; every rhombus is a parallelogram — but none of these relationships work in reverse. Not every rectangle is a square, and not every parallelogram is a rhombus.
workedExampleContent:
Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 80°, 95°, and 100°. Find the fourth angle.

Step 1: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is (4 − 2) × 180° = 360°.
Step 2: Add the three known angles: 80° + 95° + 100° = 275°.
Step 3: Subtract from the total: 360° − 275° = 85°.

The fourth angle is 85°.

---

Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 156°. How many sides does the polygon have?

Step 1: At each vertex, the interior and exterior angles form a linear pair: interior + exterior = 180°.
Step 2: So the exterior angle = 180° − 156° = 24°.
Step 3: For a regular polygon, number of sides = 360° ÷ each exterior angle.
Step 4: Number of sides = 360° ÷ 24° = 15.

The polygon has 15 sides.

---

In parallelogram PQRS, angle P = 70°. Find angle Q (adjacent to P) and angle R (opposite to P).

Step 1: Adjacent angles in a parallelogram are supplementary, so angle Q = 180° − 70° = 110°.
Step 2: Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal, so angle R = angle P = 70°.

Angle Q = 110°, angle R = 70°.
